diagrams.title: Deployment Models: Responsibility and Isolation
diagrams.subtitle: From on-premises to cloud, then IaC and OT: click each model to see what changes in security.

nodes.label: On-premises
nodes.detail: The organization owns and administers servers, network, and storage. It bears the full burden: patching, power, backups, recovery.
nodes.exam: Full control does not mean guaranteed security: the maintenance burden remains entirely yours.

nodes.label: Public cloud
nodes.detail: The provider manages the infrastructure; the customer retains data, identities, applications, and configuration. Running without an OS to maintain is the serverless variant.
nodes.exam: Customer misconfiguration remains the number one cause of cloud exposure.

nodes.label: Private / community cloud
nodes.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to one organization or shared by a community of peers. Stronger control, higher cost, peer trust governance.
nodes.exam: Community cloud = trust between organizations in the same group.

nodes.label: Hybrid
nodes.detail: Combination of on-premises and cloud connected via VPN, dedicated interconnect, or federated identity. The junction is an additional trust boundary.
nodes.exam: In a hybrid scenario, look for controls at the junction, not just in the cloud.

nodes.label: IaC / microservices
nodes.detail: Infrastructure is described in versioned files; applications are split into services communicating via APIs. Control becomes code review and drift detection.
nodes.exam: Concepts from objective §3.1, absent from the four provided books.

nodes.label: OT / air-gapped
nodes.detail: Industrial systems isolated from the Internet: availability and safety come first, transfers via controlled media, active scans prohibited.
nodes.exam: Physical segmentation offers the strongest isolation; logical segmentation depends on configuration.

quiz.question: Which model leaves data and configuration responsibility with the customer while delegating infrastructure?
